articles.title: SpaceX catches the Starship to end Flight 15

top_comments: Starship is, essentially, Space Shuttle done right: fully reusable booster without solid boosters (avoids Challenger disaster) and orbiter stacked on top instead of on the side (avoid Columbia disaster).The original designs for the Space Shuttle had the booster (with wings!) return to the launch site, but the cost for two new crewed vehicles was too large, so they scaled it back to the compromised version.Even more revolutionary, compared to Shuttle, Starship is built on an assembly line. They can build a booster ever 4 weeks and a ship every 2 weeks.The future we were promised in the 1970s is about to become real.

If the heat shield holds up then this changes everything. Next step is double catch and re-flying the same ships and catching again, then payloads to orbit become significantly cheaper opening a new era in space flight.

Huge congratulations to the engineering team on this one! It's been quite interesting to watch the evolution of Starship. Had they put another couple of tonnes of propellant and oxidizer on the Booster they might have caught both of them. It is still unclear to me what the final mass fraction to orbit will work out to be, but something that is 100% re-usable is better than something 60% reusable[1].[1] Estimate of Falcon 9's booster + fairings being 60% (by cost, not by mass) of the launch package.

articles.title: Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages
articles.summary: Lovable apps expose passport details and more than 200K private messages

top_comments: Hi, I’m the author of this blog post. I submitted it to HN two weeks ago, but it didn’t gain much traction, so I’m glad to see it resubmitted. Happy to answer any questions, though I think the situation is fairly self-explanatory.

The part people are ignoring is Supabase's culpability in this matter: https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/4547This was supposedly fixed on October 30, but there are reports floating around that for existing projects, the defaults still apply.Lovable deserves some heat for using this, but this was a choice that was made by Supabase many years ago to support making it easier to onboard potential customers, a deliberate tradeoff of less onboarding pain for less security.

Igor here, Head of Security at Lovable. Thanks to the Crissy Field team for their work. The root cause in these apps was insufficent Row-Level Security, which is exactly what our scanning is built to catch. We scan every app automatically before publish and offer a deeper SAST scan, both free for all users. When we flag findings, users can select “Fix” and Lovable will help resolve them. They can also enable auto-fix, which resolves security findings in the background, and block publishing entirely when there are critical findings.When an app has end users, security is a key part of the product. That’s why we keep investing in making security tools better and easier to use, taking on as much of the security load as we can and fixing more issues automatically.I personally believe that making security accessible is what leads to making software accessible. We’re committed to both.You can read more about our approach: https://lovable.dev/blog/find-it-fix-it-ship-it

Total KDE fan and that's all I run at home. It's an interesting study also in desktop environment and software written in C++ and just how hard it is to get something that works for most people. Mistakes, corrections, building the basic blocks like Qt in the early days and keeping a bunch of people with differing cultures / tastes / backgrounds/needs motivated to make it better every day - fascinating achievement.Thank you KDE folks - I contribute in terms of bug reports and attempts at fixes sometimes but this time I am signing up for a monthly donation - I encourage people to do what they can to keep a good thing going! https://kde.org/donate/

KDE is amazing. Outstanding performance, outstanding design, and endlessly configurable. But the most amazing thing of all is that you've achieved this while competing against teams like Microsoft's or Apple's, which spend millions of euros and are made up of thousands of people.Congratulations, team. Here's to 30 more years.

KDE is how desktops should be. 'The Year of the Linux' is NOW, a few years ago. Linux and KDE have given me not only freedom over my own hardware, but freedom over how I interact with my desktops. Once you know the shortcuts, things become so much more fun. Much love to the KDE team.Linux life, yo.

articles.title: A family tree of software job titles
articles.summary: A family tree of software job titles

top_comments: Recently I spoke to someone who wanted to know what they should call themselves seeing as they never learned software development, formally or otherwise, but that's not stopping them from releasing AI-powered Python projects in GitHub. I suggested Project Manager, but they took offense to that because (I think) they wanted to hear Software Engineer in order to apply to those jobs. My counter-argument was that, legal rules aside, a S.E. should be able to differentiate good code from bad, but my suggestion wasn't super well received.The point being: I'm always amazed at the cross-purpose impulse of arguing "the title is not important" while, simultaneously, really wanting to use the title.

Scrum and Agile seem to be dying. I had a Product Owner and Scrum Master cert for years on my resume but i've dropped it from my current. Feels now like the ancient webmaster title of the mid 90s. Made for another timeline which is not more relevant.DevOps is another sad story as it was a saner approach to get people skilled for both dev and ops but turns out people don't like learning new skills as much as they claim. So its meaning differed from org to org and even within the same company.

So far in my career:- DevOps Engineer (Junior, Senior, Staff)- Systems Development Engineer- DevOps Team Manager- Cloud Infrastructure Engineer- Site Reliability Engineer (+Lead)All have been meaningless except for Cloud Infrastructure Engineer. The rest described a generalist who knows how to deal with ambiguity and (usually) has the trust with things like AWS root account credentials. Most organisations have no idea what real DevOps is. If they did, they wouldn’t hire for a “DevOps Engineer”

Thanks for this! I've been trying to get local training working on Fedora with ROCm for a while now, and this is the first project that ran end-to-end on my RX 7600 XT 16GB.The whole reason for me buying the card was to play around with deep learning and models, so it's awesome to have a stepping off point now!No CUDA meant ROCm surprisingly just worked with JAX.Gotchas for anyone with a 7600 XT: it needed two env vars, HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=11.0.0 because JAX's plugin rejects gfx1102, and XLA_FLAGS=--xla_gpu_enable_triton_gemm=false to stop a GPU hang.I'm on Fedora 45 with the in-kernel amdgpu driver, rootless podman and AMD's rocm/jax image (ROCm 10.1, JAX 0.11.1). Nothing ROCm is installed on the host, which is nice.Container setup is in a PR if it helps anyone: https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/deepseek-v3-jax/pull/1
